Chapter 1 — Searching for Belonging in a World of Masks.
Have you ever found yourself sitting alone, maybe late in the afternoon, and wondered what it really means to belong? In Mexico, that feeling isn’t just some passing thought—it’s actually woven into everyday life. There’s this quiet sense of standing just outside the circle, of not quite fitting in, and it shapes how people move, speak, and even laugh. You can see it in the way neighbors greet each other—always with a bit of reserve. Or how, at a party, laughter sometimes feels a little guarded, almost as if there’s something hidden underneath.
Growing up in this kind of world, you learn pretty quickly that showing too much of yourself can feel risky. It’s almost like putting on invisible armor every morning—a careful way of speaking, a habit of holding back, never quite letting people in. It’s not about being fake. It’s about protecting yourself, because the world can be unpredictable. So you learn to guard your true self, to present a version that fits in and doesn’t attract too much attention.
Picture a family gathering. There’s a young man, joking and teasing, always quick with a smile. But underneath, he’s careful. He’s learned that opening up—really showing his hopes or worries—can be met with silence, or worse, with teasing that stings. So, he shares only what feels safe. And honestly, he’s not alone. It’s something almost everyone around him does, often without even realizing it.
Living this way—always keeping certain parts hidden—creates a kind of solitude that goes deeper than just being alone. It’s the kind of solitude that comes from not being fully seen, not even by the people closest to you. After a while, it becomes second nature. People get really good at reading the room, sensing when to speak up, when to stay quiet, knowing exactly which parts of themselves to reveal and which to keep tucked away.
And this isn’t just personal—it shapes the whole culture. It colors how people deal with authority, how they celebrate, and even how they grieve. You see it in the huge festivals—all the color and noise, everyone coming together. But then, when the party’s over and everything quiets down, those old masks slip back on, and that familiar distance returns.
Most people don’t talk about this directly. Instead, it shows up in the little things. Like the way a shopkeeper greets you—always polite, always just a bit formal. Or how a child answers questions with just enough to satisfy, but not enough to invite more. It’s almost like a dance—getting close, then pulling back. There’s that constant push and pull: wanting to be part of something bigger, but needing to protect yourself from being hurt or misunderstood.
This search for belonging—and the solitude that comes with it—might not be unique to Mexico, but here, it has its own flavor. It’s tied to history, to the stories people tell about themselves and their country, to the long shadows of conquest and revolution. In some ways, this solitude becomes both a burden and a source of strength—a way to get by in a world that doesn’t always feel safe.
And as the day ends and the city quiets down, that feeling is still there. There’s comfort in the familiar rituals, in knowing that everyone’s playing the same game. But there’s also a longing—a hope for real connection, for understanding, for that rare moment when the masks can finally come off, and the true self can be seen.
